guides.title: Gut and brain, in conversation
guides.lead: The gut is a sensory, immune and chemical partner of the brain. Serotonin helps carry that conversation, alongside nerves, precursors, hormones and microbial products.

sections.title: One molecule, several jobs
sections.text: About 90–95% of body serotonin is made in the intestine, predominantly by enterochromaffin cells. The brain and a smaller population of enteric neurons also make serotonin. In the gut it helps coordinate movement, secretion, sensation and immune activity. Which receptor is activated, and where, determines the response.

sections.title: From local release to a message in a nerve
sections.text: An enterochromaffin cell releases serotonin near the intestinal lining. Serotonin activates receptors on a sensory fibre; electrical activity then carries information toward the brainstem. Vagal nerve recordings demonstrate serotonin-sensitive responses. Anatomical work in mouse small intestine supports local diffusion between serotonin-containing cells and vagal endings. A separate fast circuit connects neuropod cells to vagal neurons using glutamate.

sections.title: Two serotonin pools, connected biology
sections.text: Brain serotonin is synthesised inside the nervous system. Serotonin itself does not meaningfully cross the blood–brain barrier, while its dietary precursor tryptophan can. Microbial and host metabolism influence precursor availability and its competing pathways. Germ-free mouse experiments show that plasma tryptophan and brain serotonin-related measures can change together, with effects depending on sex and developmental timing.

sections.title: Platelets carry the peripheral pool
sections.text: Platelets absorb serotonin from blood through the SERT transporter and store it, producing little themselves. Activation releases this reservoir into vascular, clotting and inflammatory responses. Its functions differ from serotonin released by brain neurons. Whole-blood serotonin therefore describes a different biological pool from serotonin activity within brain circuits.

sections.title: Immune signals, metabolites and hormones
sections.text: Microbes influence gut immune cells and barrier biology. Their products also affect distant tissues: short-chain fatty acid experiments in mice connect the microbial environment with microglial development and function. Enteroendocrine responses add chemical and neural routes. Together these pathways allow changes in gut activity to reach nervous-system biology without requiring serotonin to move from gut to brain.

sections.title: The brain also changes the gut
sections.text: Autonomic nerves and the hormonal stress system influence motility, secretion and immune activity. These changes alter conditions experienced by gut microbes. Germ-free and colonisation studies in mice demonstrate a connection between early microbial exposure and the later hormonal stress response. A body–brain map is therefore a loop with several routes and timescales.

guides.title: Food cultures around the world
guides.lead: Place belongs in the evidence. Food traditions, living conditions, medicines and access to care shape the communities that researchers measure.

sections.title: Grains, pulses and fermentation across Asia
sections.text: Rice, pulses and microbial starters make very different foods: idli in South Asia, koji-based fermentations in Japan, and fermented rice preparations across Southeast Asia. The FAO regional chapter follows the preparation methods and microbial chemistry. Our fermentation notes explore koji, miso and tempeh in more detail.

sections.title: Mediterranean tables and European ferments
sections.text: Vegetables, pulses, grains, olive oil and shared meals sit within a wider tradition of growing, preserving and eating food. UNESCO follows that cultural setting across southern Europe and North Africa. Yoghurt, kefir and sourdough offer further routes into the organisms and enzymes involved in familiar foods.

sections.title: Maize and microbial food traditions in the Americas
sections.text: Pozol and chicha show how maize becomes a substrate for mixed microbial communities. The FAO Latin American chapter describes preparation practices and the organisms studied in these foods, with references for deeper reading.

sections.title: Pacific foods, seasons and preservation
sections.text: Breadfruit, taro and other locally grown foods connect meals to island environments and seasonal harvests. The University of Hawai‘i guide describes regional food names and preparation, including fermented breadfruit preservation. Pasifika Plates brings local ingredients into everyday recipes.

sections.title: African food traditions and dietary experiments
sections.text: Injera, ogi, kisra and other grain fermentations offer distinct microbial ecosystems and food-processing techniques. A two-week dietary exchange between African American and rural South African adults measured changes in microbial chemistry and colonic tissue biomarkers. African research portals connect these questions with locally led studies and source data.

sections.title: Food cultures move with people
sections.text: Researchers studied Hmong and Karen communities in Thailand and the United States, including people sampled before and after migration. Microbial diversity and carbohydrate-processing functions changed across migration and generations. Following food, medicines and living conditions over time helps explain how a community changes as people make new homes.

guides.title: How a gut community grows
guides.lead: The microbiome develops alongside a child. Its changing functions connect feeding, microbial transmission, immune development and growth.

sections.title: A changing ecosystem
sections.text: Early communities assemble as infants encounter microbes from people and their surroundings. Feeding changes the resources available to those organisms. The developing gut, microbial community and immune system influence one another; age is part of the biological context of a sample.

sections.title: Follow children through time
sections.text: TEDDY followed 903 children from three to 46 months. Its repeated samples showed developmental, transitional and more stable phases over that period. Breast-milk exposure was a strong correlate of community structure, alongside birth mode, geography and household exposures. These are trajectories observed within the studied cohort, rather than a universal timetable for every child.

sections.title: From describing development to supporting growth
sections.text: A trial in Bangladeshi children with moderate acute malnutrition tested a food designed around microbial development. The researchers measured growth, plasma proteins and stool taxa together. This gives a concrete route from a food formulation through community changes to an outcome that matters to a child.

sections.title: The next layer to explore
sections.text: Milk glycans, microbial sharing within families, antibiotic exposure and community recovery create several different research routes. A useful early-life reference records feeding, age, location and clinical setting alongside every study so that readers can follow the relevant population.

guides.title: Medicines meet the microbiome
guides.lead: A medicine enters a chemically active ecosystem. Gut microbes can transform the drug, while the drug can change the microbial community.

sections.title: An enzyme can change a dose’s journey
sections.text: Microbial enzymes can turn a medicine into a different molecule before or during absorption. The consequence depends on the particular reaction: activity, transport and toxicity can change. A systematic screen tested 271 oral drugs against 76 gut bacteria and connected transformations to microbial genes.

sections.title: Digoxin shows why strain-level detail matters
sections.text: Some Eggerthella lenta strains inactivate the cardiac drug digoxin. Researchers identified a cytochrome-encoding operon associated with this reaction; non-metabolising strains lacked it. In colonised mice, dietary protein changed microbial metabolism and measured drug concentrations. This makes a specific gene and reaction more informative than the species label alone.

sections.title: The traffic runs both ways
sections.text: A laboratory screen of more than 1,000 marketed drugs found growth inhibition among gut strains from medicines aimed at human targets as well as antibiotics. The results identify candidate selective pressures worth investigating alongside the concentrations actually reached in the intestine.

sections.title: Connect the experiment to the patient
sections.text: Follow the parent drug, microbial product, responsible enzyme, intestinal compartment and measured host exposure. Then ask whether the transformation changes efficacy or adverse effects in people. UCT’s pharmacogenomics programme adds an African research perspective on differences in treatment response.

guides.title: Reading a microbiome test
guides.lead: Begin with the sample and the measurement. Then follow how a DNA sequence becomes a name, a percentage and a biological question.

sections.title: From stool to sequences
sections.text: A stool sample captures material leaving the bowel at a particular time. Extraction releases DNA, sequencing reads parts of it, and a reference database helps assign names. Sampling and laboratory methods shape the resulting profile. A stool sample does not give the same view as sampling mucus, the small intestine or a tissue surface.

sections.title: 16S and shotgun answer different questions
sections.text: 16S sequencing targets a marker gene used to profile bacteria and archaea. Short reads are commonly grouped as amplicon sequence variants, or ASVs, and then assigned taxonomic names. An ASV is a sequence feature: multiple variants can come from one organism, and some organisms share the measured sequence. A report containing thousands of features therefore does not establish thousands of distinct bacterial species in that person. Shotgun metagenomics samples DNA more broadly, supporting gene and finer taxonomic profiling when depth and reference coverage permit.

sections.title: A percentage needs its denominator
sections.text: Suppose a sample contains 10 units of one organism and 90 units of others: the first organism contributes 10%. If the others double while the first stays at 10, its reported share falls to about 5%. Nothing has removed those original 10 units. Cell counting, spike-ins and targeted quantitative assays offer routes to estimating absolute abundance. Sequencing alone mainly describes the sampled DNA mixture.

sections.title: Connect a result to a question
sections.text: For a useful comparison, record the assay, sampled gene region, database version, collection conditions, recent medicines, symptoms, stool form and dietary changes. Gene detection describes metabolic capacity; a metabolite assay measures a chemical pool; an isotope experiment can trace movement. A proposed clinical use then needs a study showing that acting on the result improves the outcome of interest.

coverage.title: Habitats and spatial ecology
coverage.text: Six anatomical habitats connect to organisms, chemistry and research. Direct intestinal sampling has an existing reading note.
coverage.next: Add a common comparison of stool, mucus, tissue and capsule samples, with matching study populations.

coverage.title: Everyday nutrition and fermentation
coverage.text: Living well and fermentation connect foods with organisms and experiments; fibre and bile-acid mechanisms expose the underlying chemistry.
coverage.next: Expand regional food traditions across the world, compare intervention duration and measured outcomes, and connect recipes to studies on the finished food.

coverage.title: Testing and measurement
coverage.text: A new guide connects samples, marker genes, ASVs, relative abundance and clinical questions. Mechanism maps explain several blood, breath and stool measurements.
coverage.next: Build an interactive relative-versus-absolute abundance example and a side-by-side assay comparison including ITS, 18S, metatranscriptomics and metabolomics.

coverage.title: Early life and development
coverage.text: A new guide links longitudinal childhood development with a microbiota-directed food trial.
coverage.next: Add maternal transmission, human milk oligosaccharides, pregnancy and infant interventions as separate evidence-led routes.

coverage.title: Microbial drug metabolism
coverage.text: A new guide traces drug transformation, strain-specific digoxin metabolism and medicines that affect bacterial growth.
coverage.next: Build enzyme-to-drug maps for digoxin, levodopa and irinotecan, including host pharmacokinetics and human outcome studies.

coverage.title: Food cultures and population research
coverage.text: A worldwide reading route connects regional food traditions, fermentation science, population comparisons and migration research.
coverage.next: Extend locally authored sources and attach country, recruitment setting and dietary context to more human reading notes.

coverage.title: Immunity and barrier biology
coverage.text: Mechanism maps connect mucus, microbial sensing, regulatory T cells, butyrate and bile-acid derivatives.
coverage.next: Add IgA, complement, antigen presentation and microbial translocation with a clear view of the tissue being studied.

coverage.title: Gut–brain communication
coverage.text: Serotonin and a dedicated gut–brain map connect neural, precursor, immune, metabolite and returning stress-control routes. A reading guide follows the experiments behind them.
coverage.next: Extend human vagal, stress-axis and immune studies; link sleep and mood interventions to specific measured outcomes.

coverage.title: Cardiometabolic, liver and kidney links
coverage.text: Bile-acid, SCFA and iron maps connect microbial chemistry to host transport and regulation.
coverage.next: Add TMA/TMAO, microbial lipids and kidney clearance; distinguish metabolic experiments from prospective disease-outcome studies.

coverage.title: Microbial therapies and clinical use
coverage.text: The C. difficile story includes a defined microbial therapy trial; the directory now links guidelines and regulator product records.
coverage.next: Create a compact intervention comparison with trial identifiers, outcomes, duration, route of delivery and country-specific clinical status.

coverage.title: Cancer and treatment response
coverage.text: The illness directory and paper library provide starting points. This is still a short treatment of a large research area.
coverage.next: Develop colorectal carcinogenesis, microbial genotoxins and immunotherapy-response routes with study-specific reading notes.

coverage.title: Ageing and later life
coverage.text: The reference directory identifies ageing programmes, with shared metabolic and immune mechanisms already mapped.
coverage.next: Add longitudinal ageing cohorts, frailty, medication burden and food interventions as a dedicated reading route.

coverage.title: Viruses, fungi, protists and worms
coverage.text: Microbes connects catalogue records to named papers, reviewed findings and related learning routes. Genus research and predicted-host context are shown separately from organism-specific matches.
coverage.next: Expand reviewed record-to-paper links, especially unnamed viral clusters and newly catalogued eukaryotes, and verify more taxonomic crosswalks.

coverage.title: Experimental methods and reproducibility
coverage.text: Study settings distinguish human cohorts, trials, cell experiments and animal work. Methods references are now searchable together.
coverage.next: Add worked comparisons of gnotobiotic experiments, organoids, culture collections and causal human interventions, with reusable study metadata.

coverage.title: Colonisation resistance and antimicrobial resistance
coverage.text: Illness stories and antibiotic-recovery notes introduce community disturbance and pathogen expansion.
coverage.next: Connect nutrient competition, resistance genes, phage transfer and pathogen reservoirs into a dedicated mechanism route.

coverage.title: Trials, datasets and scientific questions
coverage.text: Canonical paper IDs connect reading notes, citation links, catalogue sources and targeted community edits.
coverage.next: Add verified trial and dataset accessions directly to more notes, and curate open questions by mechanism and population.
